title: State Design Matters: How Representations Shape Dynamic Reasoning in Large Language Models
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) move from static reasoning tasks toward dynamic environments, their success depends on the ability to navigate and respond to an environment that changes as they interact at inference time. An underexplored factor in these settings is the representation of the state. Holding model parameters fixed, we systematically vary three key aspects: (1) state granularity (long form versus summary), (2) structure (natural language versus symbolic), and (3) spatial grounding (text-only versus images or textual map encodings) across sequential decision-making benchmarks. We find that trajectory summarisation improves performance by reducing noise and stabilising long-horizon reasoning. Second, natural language representations are the most robust across models, whereas structured encodings help mainly for models with strong code or structured output priors, such as JSON schemas. Third, while image-inputs show some benefit, text-based spatial encodings prove most effective. This advantage stems not from the spatial information itself, but from the act of construction, which compels the model to perform the spatial reasoning that static input does not elicit. Overall, we demonstrate that design choices for representing state are a decisive factor in performance, distinct from the availability of information itself. We note, however, that even with improved representations, current LLMs and VLMs remain brittle over long horizons, particularly when they must synthesise information to manage multiple subtasks to reach a goal.

title: A Monosemantic Attribution Framework for Stable Interpretability in Clinical Neuroscience Transformer-Based Language Models
abstract: Interpretability remains a key challenge for deploying language models (LM) in clinical settings such as progression diagnosis of Alzheimer disease, where early and trustworthy predictions are essential. Existing attribution methods exhibit high inter-method variability and unstable explanations due to the polysemantic nature of Transformer-Based LM and LLM representations, while mechanistic interpretability approaches lack direct alignment with model inputs and outputs and do not provide explicit importance scores. We introduce a unified interpretability framework that integrates attributional and mechanistic perspectives through monosemantic feature extraction. By constructing a monosemantic embedding space at the level of an transformer-based LM layer and optimizing the framework to explicitly reduce inter-method variability, our approach produces stable input-level importance scores and highlights salient features via a decompressed representation of the layer of interest, advancing the safe and trustworthy application of LMs in cognitive health and neurodegenerative disease.

title: Snow Goose Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Swarm optimization algorithms, by simulating the cooperative behavior of biological groups in nature, exhibit strong robustness and adaptability in complex optimization problems. However, most existing optimization algorithms based on animal behavior still rely on static or semi-static leadership structures, single-point optimal guidance strategies, and weak temporal memory mechanisms, making them prone to premature convergence and search stagnation in high-dimensional or multimodal problems. To address this, this paper proposes a novel swarm optimization method—the Snow Goose Optimization Algorithm (SGOA). This algorithm uses the formation coordination, leader rotation, airflow perception, and path correction behaviors of snow geese during long-distance migration as biological prototypes. By introducing mechanisms such as airflow shadow prediction, asymmetric formation self-evolution, leader fatigue resignation, migration turnaround search, and fuzzy endpoint attraction, it achieves joint control over search direction, search scale, and search stability. The proposed algorithm significantly enhances the dynamism and diversity of the search process without relying on complex parameters, providing a new approach to solving complex continuous optimization problems.

title: Patentability of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Inventions
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies are rapidly transforming various industries, including healthcare, finance, transportation, and manufacturing. As AI-based systems increasingly generate innovative solutions, questions arise regarding their protection under existing patent laws. Traditional patent frameworks were primarily designed for human inventors and mechanical inventions, creating uncertainty when applied to AI and ML innovations. This paper examines the patentability of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning inventions by analyzing core patentability requirements such as novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability. It discusses key legal challenges including algorithm patent exclusion, inventorship issues, and disclosure requirements. The study further provides a comparative analysis of patent approaches adopted in India, the United States, and Europe. The paper concludes by emphasizing the need for updated legal guidelines and international harmonization to effectively address emerging challenges in AI-related patent protection while encouraging innovation and safeguardin

title: Rethinking Soft Compression in Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Query-Conditioned Selector Perspective
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) effectively grounds Large Language Models (LLMs) with external knowledge and is widely applied to Web-related tasks. However, its scalability is hindered by excessive context length and redundant retrievals. Recent research on soft context compression aims to address this by encoding long documents into compact embeddings, yet they often underperform non-compressed RAG due to their reliance on auto-encoder-like full-compression that forces the encoder to compress all document information regardless of relevance to the input query. In this work, we conduct an analysis on this paradigm and reveal two fundamental limitations: (I) Infeasibility, full-compression conflicts with the LLM's downstream generation behavior; and (II) Non-necessity: full-compression is unnecessary and dilutes task-relevant information density. Motivated by these insights, we introduce SeleCom, a selector-based soft compression framework for RAG that redefines the encoder's role as query-conditioned information selector. The selector is decoder-only and is trained with a massive, diverse and difficulty-graded synthetic QA dataset with curriculum learning. Extensive experiments show that SeleCom significantly outperforms existing soft compression approaches and achieves competitive or superior performance to non-compression baselines, while reducing computation and latency by 33.8%~84.6%.

title: Common Tern Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Swarm intelligence optimization algorithms typically solve complex optimization problems by simulating the cooperative behavior of groups of organisms in nature. However, most existing methods rely on instantaneous optimal information or direct positional guidance between individuals, making them prone to premature convergence in noisy environments or multi-peaked search spaces. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel swarm intelligence optimization method—the Common Tern Optimization Algorithm. This algorithm uses the foraging behavior of Common Tern flocks as a biological prototype, introducing mechanisms such as flock circling search, perceptual lag integration, directional consensus assessment, and hierarchical descent decision-making to construct a flock search model with a cognitive hierarchy. Unlike traditional algorithms that rely on the current position's optimal solution as the driving force, the Common Tern Optimization Algorithm uses flock directional consensus and its credibility as the primary decision-making basis, thus achieving a balance between stable exploration and phased transitions. Theoretical analysis shows that this algorithm has significant advantages in suppressing false consensus, reducing the risk of premature convergence, and improving search robustness.

title: Black Stork Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Swarm optimization algorithms, by simulating the collaborative behavior of individuals in nature, exhibit strong adaptability in continuous optimization and complex search problems. However, most existing algorithms suffer from problems such as memory loss, over-convergence, and simplistic stagnation handling mechanisms during the search process. To address these shortcomings, this paper proposes a novel swarm optimization method—the Black Stork Optimization Algorithm. This algorithm is modeled after the low-density foraging, long-term memory, and event-driven migration behavior of black storks in wetland environments, constructing a search mechanism from three levels: behavioral, informational, and structural. The algorithm achieves long-term accumulation of experience in the search space by introducing a wetland memory map, alleviates crowding and conflict among individuals near the optimal area through behavioral inhibition mechanisms, and selectively reconstructs the population structure during long-term stagnation by triggering search strategies through rare events. This method constructs an optimization framework with strong interpretability and scalability without relying on complex mathematical assumptions or additional experimental control, providing a new approach to behavioral modeling of swarm intelligence algorithms.

title: Optimizing the Content Generation Mechanism of Cross-Cultural Brand Communication Using Web Algorithms in Converged Media Environment
abstract: In order to enhance the effectiveness of cross-cultural brand communication, this paper proposes the Transformer model using Self-Attention mechanism and Multi-Head Attention mechanism for content generation. Combined with the pointer network, the TP model based on the optimized Transformer model is designed. Conduct ROUGE score comparison experiments between the TP model and five mainstream copywriting generation models to evaluate their performance effects. To further validate the usability of the content generated by the TP model, this paper uses a questionnaire to analyze the audience's agreement. The results show that the performance comparison between the TP model and the AAT model, which has the best performance among the five comparison models, increases the scores in the ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L evaluation functions by 0.00982, 0.00143, and 0.00953 in that order. The average emotional resonance identity, average value confirmation identity, and average sharing and Diffusion recognition were 3.9304, 3.9806, and 4.0202, respectively, indicating that the use of the TP model to generate marketing copy can trigger audience resonance and brand recognition, providing new ideas and methods for brand cross-cultural communication.

title: South American Capybara Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Swarm optimization algorithms, due to their simple structure, robustness, and adaptability to complex nonlinear problems, have been widely applied in continuous optimization, feature selection, and parameter optimization. However, most existing swarm optimization algorithms based on animal behavior generally adopt the homogeneity assumption in individual modeling, meaning that all individuals follow the exact same update rules. This limits the algorithm's ability to represent complex search spaces and easily leads to premature convergence or rapid loss of diversity during the search process. To address this, this paper proposes a novel swarm optimization method—the South American capybara optimization algorithm. Inspired by the social behavior and environmental adaptation characteristics of South American capybaras, this algorithm systematically improves the algorithm's ability to balance exploration and exploitation by constructing a hierarchical group structure, a multi-state search mechanism, a historical water memory model, and a parameter adaptation strategy based on information entropy. This paper analyzes the algorithm's update mechanism, parameter evolution process, and overall dynamic characteristics in detail from a rigorous mathematical modeling perspective, and discusses the algorithm's convergence behavior from the perspectives of probability theory and information theory. Theoretical analysis shows that the algorithm converges to a stable solution domain with a high probability under finite iteration conditions, while effectively avoiding the premature convergence problem common in traditional swarm intelligence algorithms.

title: Metode Finite Mixture Partial Least Square Untuk Mengatasi Heterogenitas Pada Model Struktural Partial Least Square
abstract: Finite Mixture Partial Least Square (FIMIX-PLS) adalah metode untuk mengungkap heterogenitas yang tidak teramati di dalam model struktural. FIMIX-PLS dapat dipakai sebagai pendekatan yang komprehensif untuk mengetahui heterogenitas dalam pemodelan jalur PLS. Metode FIMIX-PLS mengidentifikasi heterogenitas data dengan memperkirakan probabilitas dari keanggotaan segmen untuk setiap observasi dan secara bersamaan memperkirakan koefisien jalur semua segmen. Pada studi kasus pengaruh predisposisi dan kebiasaan terhadap tekanan darah pasien hipertensi, sehingga menghasilkan anggota kelompok yang lebih homogen berdasarkan hubungan antar variabel laten. Pada penelitian ini ,jumlah segmen terbaik hasil dari FIMIX-PLS dipilih berdasarkan nilai kriteria dari AIC dan EN. Tujuan penelitian ini yaitu mendeteksi heterogenitas pada model struktural PLS menggunakan metode FIMIX-PLS pada studi kasus pengaruh predisposisi dan kebiasaan terhadap tekanan darah pasien hipertensi dan mengetahui jumlah segmentasi terbaik dari hasil FIMIX- PLS berdasarkan nilai kriteria dari AIC dan EN. Variabel predisposisi diukur oleh 6 indikator yaitu jenis kelamin, keterbatasan mobilitas, penyakit penyerta, psikolo- gis, suhu tubuh dan usia. Variabel kebiasaan pasien diukur oleh 5 indikator alkohol, diet oral, merokok dan olahraga. Variabel tekanan darah diukur oleh 2 variabel indikator distolik dan sistolik. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan kajian hetoreginitas dengan dengan FIMIX-PLS menghasilkan segmentasi yang menunjukkan adanya heterogenitas. Segmentasi terbaik pada K=5 dengan nilai AIC terendah yaitu sebesar 175,947 dengan nilai EN sebesar 0,610.

title: Quantum-Inspired Algorithms beyond Unitary Circuits: the Laplace Transform
abstract: Quantum-inspired algorithms can deliver substantial speedups over classical state-of-the-art methods by executing quantum algorithms with tensor networks on conventional hardware. Unlike circuit models restricted to unitary gates, tensor networks naturally accommodate non-unitary maps. This flexibility lets us design quantum-inspired methods that start from a quantum algorithmic structure, yet go beyond unitarity to achieve speedups. Here we introduce a tensor-network approach to compute the discrete Laplace transform, a non-unitary, aperiodic transform (in contrast to the Fourier transform). We encode a length-$N$ signal on two paired $n$-qubit registers and decompose the overall map into a non-unitary exponential Damping Transform followed by a Quantum Fourier Transform, both compressed in a single matrix-product operator. This decomposition admits strong MPO compression to low bond dimension resulting in significant acceleration. We demonstrate simulations up to $N=2^{30}$ input data points, with up to $2^{60}$ output data points, and quantify how bond dimension controls runtime and accuracy, including precise and efficient pole identification.

title: Revolutionizing Research Workflows: A Comprehensive Framework for ChatGPT Applications in Academia and R&D
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) redefine the boundaries of human-machine interaction, their integration into scientific workflows offers a paradigm shift for academia, research, and industrial development. This chapter presents a comprehensive framework for applying ChatGPT across the entire Research and Development (R&D) lifecycle, moving beyond basic text generation to establish a practical taxonomy of AI applications in specialized domains. We analyze the model's operational utility in critical areas including the construction of material and chemical databases, the development of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for laboratory instruments, and the automation of data processing and visualization. Furthermore, the text details methodologies for leveraging conversational AI as a "virtual assistant" in competitive academic processes, such as optimizing grant funding proposals, navigating technology transfer and intellectual property protection, and streamlining conference management. By providing specific use-cases—ranging from interpreting complex experimental data to debugging software code—this work serves as an essential guide for researchers, educators, and innovators seeking to enhance productivity, accuracy, and scientific discovery through the responsible adoption of AI.

title: Ż Collapse Lab: Reproducible Structural Interventions for Preventing LLM Collapse (Preprint)
abstract: Ż Collapse Lab is a fully reproducible experimental pipeline (vSAVE-1.1.1) for detecting and preventing LLM collapse under stress-test decoding. We define collapse operationally via a fixed set of measurable failure signals (π-threshold exceedance, repetition, too-short termination, and max-length saturation), and apply a structural intervention that resets the context state to recover generation stability. This release provides a preprint + reproducibility package including the paper, fixed prompts (5 pillars), calibration artifacts, summary results, and scripts to regenerate Table 1. Key idea (vSAVE) Baseline vs Controlled differ only by whether structural intervention is enabled. All hyperparameters, thresholds, and prompts are fixed for reproducibility. Results are aggregated via a deterministic pipeline: runs → summary → table. Experimental setting (fixed) Model: GPT-2 (117M) Decoding: max_new_tokens=512, temperature=1.2, top_p=0.95 Seeds: 0–499 Pillars: HUM / STEM / ETH / TEMP / META Conditions: baseline / controlled Collapse parameters: epsilon_pi=0.85, k_consecutive=3, min_tokens=64, rep_ngram=3, rep_threshold=0.20 Controlled intervention budget: max_interventions=5, context reset ratio 0.70 Contents Preprint PDF (main paper) vSAVE reproducibility README/spec Runner script for generating runs Calibration artifacts (calib.json, calibration corpus) Pillar prompt sets (20 blocks × 5 domains) Summary-level results (runs_summary_all.csv) Script to regenerate Table 1 (make_table1.py) and the generated markdown table (table1.md) (Optional) SES compatibility implementation for π / normalization references Quickstart (reproduce Table 1 from provided summary) python make_table1.py \ --summary_csv runs_summary_all.csv \ --out_csv table1.csv \ --out_md table1.md \ --bootstrap 20000 \ --seed 0 Full reproduction (generate runs, then summarize, then Table 1) Use the included runner and the vSAVE README to reproduce the full 5,000-run study (5 pillars × 2 modes × 500 seeds). Notes This release is provided as a preprint / technical report package intended for transparent archiving and reproducibility. Author: Masayuki Okita (Independent Researcher) Acknowledgment: ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used for drafting and code assistance; experimental design choices and validation were performed by the author. The goal of this release is not to maximize benchmark performance, but to provide a controlled, versioned, and fully replayable collapse-prevention evaluation protocol. We release this package as a preprint/technical report to support transparent archiving and reproducible evaluation.

title: [Diagnosis and treatment of colorectal cancer in the era of artificial intelligence: review and prospect].
abstract: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved groundbreaking progress in the field of medicine, particularly in the diagnosis and treatment of colorectal cancer (CRC). In terms of data analysis, AI-assisted diagnosis and treatment has significantly improved the sensitivity of colonoscopy and the accuracy of pathological diagnosis, thereby providing robust support for CRC diagnosis. Regarding data utilization, AI demonstrates unique advantages in precision medicine, prognosis prediction, and recurrence follow-up, leveraging its powerful data processing capabilities to explore more possibilities for CRC treatment. AI is increasingly becoming a pillar of the medical field. However, AI still faces significant challenges, including a shortage of high-quality datasets, barriers in medical insurance reimbursement, and insufficient algorithm generalization. The challenges confronting AI have gradually shifted from technical issues such as algorithm optimization and sample collection during the initial development phase to societal concerns including ethical review, insurance reimbursement barriers, and economic benefits during the application phase.

title: Agentic AI for Self-Driving Laboratories in Soft Matter: Taxonomy, Benchmarks,and Open Challenges
abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) close the loop between experiment design, automated execution, and data-driven decision making, and they provide a demanding testbed for agentic AI under expensive actions, noisy and delayed feedback, strict feasibility and safety constraints, and non-stationarity. This survey uses soft matter as a representative setting but focuses on the AI questions that arise in real laboratories. We frame SDL autonomy as an agent environment interaction problem with explicit observations, actions, costs, and constraints, and we use this formulation to connect common SDL pipelines to established AI principles. We review the main method families that enable closed loop experimentation, including Bayesian optimization and active learning for sample efficient experiment selection, planning and reinforcement learning for long horizon protocol optimization, and tool using agents that orchestrate heterogeneous instruments and software. We emphasize verifiable and provenance aware policies that support debugging, reproducibility, and safe operation. We then propose a capability driven taxonomy that organizes systems by decision horizon, uncertainty modeling, action parameterization, constraint handling, failure recovery, and human involvement. To enable meaningful comparison, we synthesize benchmark task templates and evaluation metrics that prioritize cost aware performance, robustness to drift, constraint violation behavior, and reproducibility. Finally, we distill lessons from deployed SDLs and outline open challenges in multi-modal representation, calibrated uncertainty, safe exploration, and shared benchmark infrastructure.

title: State Estimation of a Moving Frequency Source From Observations at Multiple Receivers
abstract: Abstract The task of position and velocity estimation of a body based on the Doppler effect, whether the body is transmitting or receiving a signal of known or unknown frequency, is a common problem arising in many different application domains. While prior works use nonlinear least-squares methods to solve the Doppler equations for positioning, such an approach requires an initial estimate to perform the initial linearization step. However, in certain scenarios (e.g., initial orbit determination), an initial estimate may not be readily available, and without a good initial estimate, the nonlinear least-squares solution may not converge. This work reformulates the Doppler-based positioning problem as a system of polynomial equations, allowing for a direct solution without any a priori state information. We then leverage homotopy continuation to obtain the global solution to the polynomial system. For an unknown transmitter (or receiver), we show that the data from six or seven receivers (or transmitters) is sufficient in the case of known or unknown frequency, respectively, to recover the unknown state up to finitely many possibilities. This technique provides a structured method for initializing nonlinear least-squares or sequential filters for further refinement of the estimated state, improving their convergence. After a brief development of the mathematics, two simple examples are provided: (1) initial orbit determination of a satellite emitting an electromagnetic signal and (2) position and velocity estimation of a vocalizing dolphin emitting an acoustic signal.

title: Privacy-Preserving Federated Spiking Neural Networks for Real-Time Target Detection in Distributed ISAC Edge Systems
abstract: This study proposes a privacy-preserving federated spiking neural network (SNN) framework for real-time target detection in integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) edge networks. The framework enables distributed vehicular nodes operating at 28 GHz to collaboratively learn from spike-based sensing data without sharing raw observations, thereby protecting sensitive location information. By combining federated learning with secure model aggregation, adaptive differential privacy, and spike-aware temporal learning, the system ensures robust privacy protection while supporting efficient learning under non-IID data and real-time constraints. Extensive experiments using data from 500 vehicles and 50,000 observations demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a high detection performance of 94.3% F1-score under strict privacy guarantees, with low inference latency and significantly reduced energy consumption. These results highlight the framework’s suitability for privacy-sensitive vehicular and smart-city applications, supporting scalable, energy-efficient, and trustworthy 6G ISAC deployment.

title: Delta-State Algebra: A Formally Verified Foundation for Transient State Computation
abstract: This preprint presents delta-state algebra, a formally verified mathematical foundation for transient state computation. The model replaces persistent architectural state with composable state differences (“deltas”), where computation is expressed as algebraic transformations composed via bitwise XOR. We show that the delta space forms an Abelian group, enabling deterministic, reversible, and order-independent computation. The paper establishes the core theoretical results underpinning this model, including: (i) group-theoretic properties of delta composition, (ii) deterministic and reversible state transitions with no hidden state, (iii) equivalence between sequential and composed delta application, (iv) computational equivalence with traditional stateful models, and (v) Turing completeness via counter machine simulation. All results are formally verified in the Lean4 proof assistant, with 92 machine-checked theorems and zero unproven obligations. These results provide a rigorous mathematical foundation for hardware architectures based on transient state computation, including ATOMiK, enabling bounded latency, parallel delta accumulation, and elimination of cache hierarchies and coherency protocols while preserving computational semantics. This preprint is released to establish priority of the mathematical foundations and to enable open academic review prior to subsequent benchmarking, hardware implementation, and peer-reviewed publication.

title: RealityStressTest : Universal Stability Benchmark for ANY Dataset
abstract: . RealityStressTest : Test de stabilité universel pour tout ensemble de données Auteur : Kevin Fradier — 2026 Licence : © 2025 Kevin Fradier — CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 Résumé exécutif RealityStressTest (RST) est un protocole universel pour mesurer la stabilité interne de n'importe quel ensemble de données face à de petites perturbations contrôlées. Il fournit un StabilityScore combinant IRD et ICME pour comparer des systèmes et des ensembles de données. Le cadre est neutre, transversal et testable , applicable à toutes les données numériques. Les résultats sont publiables et reproductibles, sans hypothèse sur la nature des données. Un leaderboard public permet de comparer automatiquement tout l'ensemble des données soumises et de générer de la visibilité immédiate. 1. Objectif Détecter et quantifier les variations internes d'un ensemble de données sous perturbation. Créer un benchmark universel pour comparer les systèmes entre eux. Rendre le protocole viral et interactif grâce à un leaderboard public. 2. Principe général Observer l’état initial des données. Appliquer une perturbation contrôlée (bruit, filtrage, changement d'échelle). Observer l'état post-perturbation. Calculateur de l'Indice de Recalibrage Différentiel (IRD) et de l'Indice de Cohérence Multi-Échelle (ICME). Combinaison IRD + ICME → Score de stabilité. StabilityScore : un nombre unique, interprétation immédiate, comparable entre les ensembles de données. 3. Mise en œuvre minimale (Python) import numpy as np class RealityStressTest: def __init__(self, data): self.data = np.asarray(data) def observe(self, window=50): n = len(self.data) return np.array([ np.mean(self.data[i:i+window]**2) for i in range(0, n - window + 1, window) ]) def perturb(self, intensity=0.01): noise = intensity * np.random.randn(len(self.data)) return RealityStressTest(self.data + noise) def IRD(self, other, window=50): s0 = self.observe(window) s1 = other.observe(window) return float(np.mean(np.abs(s1 - s0))) def ICME(self, other, window=50): s0 = self.observe(window) s1 = other.observe(window) return float(np.std(s1 - s0)) # écart-type multi-échelle def StabilityScore(self, other, alpha=0.7, beta=0.3, window=50): return alpha*self.IRD(other, window) + beta*self.ICME(other, window) # ---- Exemple ---- data = np.random.randn(10000) RST0 = RealityStressTest(data) RST1 = RST0.perturb(intensity=0.01) score = RST0.StabilityScore(RST1) print("StabilityScore =", score) 4. Jeux de données de démonstration Ensemble de données Effilage Score (exemple) LIGO public Onde gravitationnelle 0,87 EEG Physionet Signaux cérébraux 0,45 Prix du Bitcoin Finance 0,61 Température climatique Climat 0,39 Intégrations GPT NLP 0,72 Images MNIST Vision 0,51 5. Classement public Soumission facile : interface web / zenedo / Streamlit Score automatique → classement immédiat Gamification : « Mon dataset vs le monde » Transparence : chaque score traçable au dataset et à l'auteur 6. Propriétés du protocole Testable : applicable à tout dataset numérique. Reproductible : mêmes données → mêmes résultats statistiques. Transversal : sciences, finance, climat, IA, physique… Minimal : dépendances externes faibles (numpy). Non interprétatif : StabilityScore = mesure, pas jugement. _____ Même mon Excel de cours sur le frigo a un StabilityScore plus stable que LIGO ! 😂💥 Testez vos données, pas vos nerfs. "Leaderboard mondial : Excel de courses = 0,91 ; LIGO = 0,87… Qui aurait cru que mes cours étaient plus fiables que le cosmos ? 😂" «Quand tu réalises que tes dépenses de cours sont plus stables que les ondes gravitationnelles… 🤯 #RealityStressTest» Challenge du jour : faites mieux que mon Excel de cours. LIGO n'y arrive pas. 😂” Auteur : Kevin Fradier — 2026 Licence : © 2025 Kevin Fradier — CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

Mise en œuvre minimale (Python) import numpy as np class RealityStressTest: def __init__(self, data): self.data = np.asarray(data) def observe(self, window=50): n = len(self.data) return np.array([ np.mean(self.data[i:i+window]**2) for i in range(0, n - window + 1, window) ]) def perturb(self, intensity=0.01): noise = intensity * np.random.randn(len(self.data)) return RealityStressTest(self.data + noise) def IRD(self, other, window=50): s0 = self.observe(window) s1 = other.observe(window) return float(np.mean(np.abs(s1 - s0))) def ICME(self, other, window=50): s0 = self.observe(window) s1 = other.observe(window) return float(np.std(s1 - s0)) # écart-type multi-échelle def StabilityScore(self, other, alpha=0.7, beta=0.3, window=50): return alpha*self.IRD(other, window) + beta*self.ICME(other, window) # ---- Exemple ---- data = np.random.randn(10000) RST0 = RealityStressTest(data) RST1 = RST0.perturb(intensity=0.01) score = RST0.StabilityScore(RST1) print("StabilityScore =", score) 4. title: Compact On-Chip Metalens Enabled Photonic Integrated Circuits for Ultrafast Fourier Transform-Based Convolutional Neural Network Acceleration
abstract: This paper demonstrates, for the first time, a compact (7.6$\times 4.6 \mu ~\mathrm{m}^{2}$) on-chip metalens integrated on a photonic integrated circuit (PIC) that performs ultrafast Fourier and inverse Fourier transforms to accelerate convolutional neural network (CNN) operations. Its powerful acceleration capability for large-scale data streams enables seamless multi-sensor integration and photonic in-sensor computing, establishing a scalable and efficient foundation for advanced integrated photonic computing.

title: D-Models and E-Models: Diversity-Stability Trade-offs in the Sampling Behavior of Large Language Models
abstract: The predictive probability of the next token (P_token) in large language models (LLMs) is inextricably linked to the probability of relevance for the next piece of information, the purchase probability of the next product, and the execution probability of the next action-all of which fall under the scope of the task-level target distribution (P_task). While LLMs are known to generate samples that approximate real-world distributions, whether their fine-grained sampling probabilities faithfully align with task requirements remains an open question. Through controlled distribution-sampling simulations, we uncover a striking dichotomy in LLM behavior, distinguishing two model types: D-models (e.g. Qwen-2.5), whose P_token exhibits large step-to-step variability and poor alignment with P_task; and E-models (e.g. Mistral-Small), whose P_token is more stable and better aligned with P_task. We further evaluate these two model types in downstream tasks such as code generation and recommendation, revealing systematic trade-offs between diversity and stability that shape task outcomes. Finally, we analyze the internal properties of both model families to probe their underlying mechanisms. These findings offer foundational insights into the probabilistic sampling behavior of LLMs and provide practical guidance on when to favor D- versus E-models. For web-scale applications, including recommendation, search, and conversational agents, our results inform model selection and configuration to balance diversity with reliability under real-world uncertainty, providing a better level of interpretation.

title: Hazel Grouse Optimization Algorithm
abstract: To address the problems of premature convergence, over-reliance on global optima, and excessive synchronicity in search behavior inherent in traditional swarm intelligence optimization algorithms for complex multimodal problems, this paper proposes a novel swarm intelligence optimization algorithm—the Hazel Grouse Optimization (HGO). Inspired by the behavioral characteristics of hazel grouse in their natural environment, such as lurking, scouting, and sudden takeoff, HGO models the optimization process as a discontinuous search system based on individual state switching and event triggering. Unlike existing methods, HGO does not rely on a single global optimum for guidance. Instead, it achieves adaptive exploration and stable development of the search space through asymmetric local information propagation, direction-trend level path memory, and weakly synchronous heterogeneous evolution mechanisms. This paper systematically presents the mathematical modeling process of HGO, detailing the individual state machine, event-driven update rules, information field construction methods, and evolutionary dynamics characteristics, providing a new research paradigm for the structured design of swarm intelligence optimization algorithms.

title: Estimating Confidentiality of Encrypted Search Systems: A Probabilistic Framework
abstract: We develop a probabilistic framework for quantifying the confidentiality of encrypted search systems based on the sampling distribution of a confidentiality statistic. Using the Bootstrap method with normal approximation, we efficiently estimate the risk of confidentiality breach, enabling proactive countermeasures. Our analysis shows how entropy of the query distribution relates to the adversary's expected accuracy, providing theoretical grounding for resilience engineering approaches to encrypted search security.

title: Harnessing Vibro-Impact Dynamics for High-Performance MEMS-Based Reservoir Computing
abstract: This work demonstrates the first physical reservoir computer based on a MEMS vibro-impact resonator. This approach harnesses the rich, nonlinear dynamics generated by periodic mechanical contact, a regime fundamentally different from the weak, continuous nonlinearity of conventional Duffing-based physical reservoir computers. Vibro-impact systems access this strong nonlinear regime with minimal physical displacement, offering a significant advantage in device scaling and complexity generation. This work uses CMOS-MEMS resoswitch, a device proven for enabling ultra-low-power operation in wireless communication systems. Benchmarked against standard tasks, including NARMA, XOR, and MNIST image classification, the vibro-impact-based system achieves comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art Duffing-based counterparts. These results are achieved with smaller training datasets, suggesting the generation of a more complex, high-dimensional state space that is highly effective for nonlinear and classification tasks.

title: UniCog: Uncovering Cognitive Abilities of LLMs through Latent Mind Space Analysis
abstract: A growing body of research suggests that the cognitive processes of large language models (LLMs) differ fundamentally from those of humans. However, existing interpretability methods remain limited in explaining how cognitive abilities are engaged during LLM reasoning. In this paper, we propose UniCog, a unified framework that analyzes LLM cognition via a latent mind space. Formulated as a latent variable model, UniCog encodes diverse abilities from dense model activations into sparse, disentangled latent dimensions. Through extensive analysis on six advanced LLMs, including DeepSeek-V3.2 and GPT-4o, we reveal a Pareto principle of LLM cognition, where a shared reasoning core is complemented by ability-specific signatures. Furthermore, we discover that reasoning failures often manifest as anomalous intensity in latent activations. These findings opens a new paradigm in LLM analysis, providing a cognition grounded view of reasoning dynamics. Finally, leveraging these insights, we introduce a latent-informed candidate prioritization strategy, which improves reasoning performance by up to 7.5% across challenging benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/milksalute/unicog.

title: Australian Dingo Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Swarm intelligence optimization algorithms, by simulating the cooperative behavior of groups of organisms in nature, exhibit strong global search capabilities and robustness in complex optimization problems. However, most existing algorithms still rely primarily on fixed control parameters, a single global optimum guidance mechanism, or simple random perturbation strategies, failing to fully characterize the situational awareness and internal regulatory behaviors exhibited by real biological groups in complex environments. To address this, this paper proposes a novel swarm intelligence optimization method—the dingo optimization algorithm. This algorithm uses the hunting behavior of dingoes in their natural environment as a biological prototype, introducing a group situational awareness mechanism, a social tension regulation mechanism, and an opportunistic raid strategy to model the search process from a group cognitive perspective. The algorithm constructs a situational vector to characterize the overall search state of the group, adaptively adjusts search behavior based on group dispersion, fitness concentration, and improved inertia, and utilizes a social tension function to constrain the spatial relationships between individuals, thereby improving convergence stability while maintaining population diversity. Theoretical analysis shows that this algorithm can achieve a dynamic balance between exploration and exploitation without complex parameter adjustments, providing a new approach for solving continuous and multimodal optimization problems.

title: [DEPRECATED]The Square-Root Scaling Law of Decoherence: A Theory of Resource Competition at the Projection Interface
abstract: Update Notice (v2) 2026/2/13 This preprint has been superseded by a significantly revised version, which has been uploaded as a separate submission. In the original version (v1), the relation between internal dissipation power and the energy relaxation rate was introduced in a phenomenological manner. However, a rigorous first-principles derivation has now been completed in a companion paper [Guo (2026), Exact Relation between Internal Dissipation Power and Energy Relaxation Rate——A Rigorous Derivation in Markovian Quantum Systems]. Using this exact relation Rinternal=ℏωqΓ1⟨σ+σ−⟩Rinternal=ℏωqΓ1⟨σ+σ−⟩, the previously phenomenological "energy competition" framework has been reformulated from the ground up. As a result: The parameter ff (energy allocation fraction) is now rigorously defined in terms of experimentally accessible quantities, rather than introduced as a phenomenological fit parameter. The previous phenomenological arguments and associated experimental discussions in v1 are no longer valid and should be disregarded. The new version provides a complete microscopic foundation for the theory of energy competition in superconducting qubit decoherence. Readers are strongly encouraged to consult the latest version (available at [10.5281/zenodo.18624328) for a comprehensive and self-contained treatment. Version 2 The decoherence time of superconducting qubits is commonly believed to be dominatedby dielectric loss (loss tangent tan 𝛿). Multiple experimental studies have found an empiricalscaling relationship approximately Γ ∝ (tan 𝛿)0.7 between the decoherence rate Γ = 1/𝑇2and tan 𝛿. Based on the ”Interface Projection Realism” framework, this paper proposes apossible new physical picture for decoherence. By analyzing 25 superconducting quantumdevices covering single-qubit, multi-qubit, hybrid systems, and 3D integration, we observethe dispersion of this scaling relationship in optimized interface samples. Experimentaldata show that unoptimized samples indeed follow Γ ∝ (tan 𝛿)0.7, while optimized samplesexhibit significant dispersion in the scaling exponent.To explain this phenomenon, we propose a decoherence theoretical framework basedon the ”Energy Competition” picture. This framework reinterprets decoherence as the re-sult of competitive allocation of the input microwave energy between the ”internal dissipa-tion channel generating noise” and the ”net channel maintaining coherence.” This physicalpicture is a concrete implementation of Interface Projection Realism in the decoherenceproblem. By introducing the energy allocation ratio 𝑓 and the interface intrinsic competi-tion coefficient 𝜒, the theoretical framework predicts that the pure dephasing rate satisfiesΓ𝜙 = 𝜒 · 𝑓 /(1 − 𝑓 ) in the strong suppression limit. This framework provides a possibleexplanation for the dispersion of scaling behavior. Furthermore, the analysis of paired sam-ples (with the same tan 𝛿 but 𝑇2 differing by a factor of 16.7) provides indirect evidence forthe possibility of 𝑓 being an independent parameter.Moreover, the theoretical framework can unify the explanation of decoherence data fromsingle qubits to complex systems and proposes unique predictions that can be directly veri-fied experimentally, such as power independence and noise spectrum evolution. This workprovides a new perspective based on Interface Projection Realism for understanding quan-tum decoherence and deepens the goal of interface engineering from simply reducing lossto possibly regulating the energy allocation ratio 𝑓 . Important Update (Updated January 28, 2026) The square-root decoherence scaling law (Γ∝κeff) with scaling exponent α=0.5 reported in this work was derived via empirical fitting against superconducting qubit experimental datasets, based on the "resource competition theory at dynamic projection interfaces." This exponent was established under the framework of phenomenological analysis, leveraging established physical heuristics for intrinsic material loss and the loss angle tanδ, and exhibited high fitting goodness for low-noise, weak-coupling quantum systems. Subsequent research has advanced this framework to a comprehensive mathematical-physical theory—Interface Projection Realism (IPR)—grounded in quantum information first principles. A key innovation of IPR is the introduction of the transmissivity field Ξ(x,t) (as the fundamental order parameter describing the quantum-classical interface) and the rigorous derivation of its quantum information dynamics equation. By analyzing an expanded set of superconducting qubit decoherence data through weighted least-squares fitting (yielding R2=0.9987, an extremely significant F-statistic of 2856.3), the universal decoherence scaling exponent is refined to α=0.792±0.008. This revised exponent corresponds to a synergy index m=4.81±0.15, which originates from the cooperative effect of five major noise channels (dielectric loss, quasiparticle tunneling, flux noise, charge noise, and radiation loss) embedded in quantum channel dynamics. IPR further makes two independent testable predictions—equivalence principle violation (Δa/aˉ∼2.3×10−9) and a first-principles calculation of dark energy density (ρΛ≈4.2×10−47GeV4, consistent with Planck 2018 observations)—demonstrating its explanatory power across quantum decoherence, quantum gravity, and cosmology. A complete account of the theoretical derivation, microphysical mechanism, and experimental corroboration is provided in our latest work: Interface Projection Realism: A Multiscale Unified Theory Based on Quantum Information Dynamics (Zenodo, Version v3, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.18400122, January 28, 2026). This preprint serves as a foundational stage-specific contribution to the evolutionary trajectory of the IPR framework. The α=0.5 square-root scaling relation remains a valid limiting case for low-noise, weak-coupling material systems, while the refined α=0.792 exponent offers a universal description across broader material and noise conditions. Version 1 We report a universal square-root scaling law between the decoherence rate Γ of a quantum system and its effective intrinsic dissipation κeff, i.e., Γ ∝ √ κeff. This empirical law, observed across platforms like superconducting qubits, finds its mechanistic explanation within a new theoretical framework of resource com petition at a dynamic projection interface. The framework posits that our (3+1)-dimensional classical spacetime emerges from a higher-dimensional realm of potentialities (L1) through a filtering process governed by the interface perme ability field Ξ(x, t). Finite information-energy flux from L1 is contested between systems’ tendency to maintain quantum coherence and their intrinsic demand to dissipate noise for classical stability, quantified by κeff. From this competition dy namics, we derive the square-root scaling law. The model further provides unified, objective descriptions of quantum measurement as channel locking and of grav ity as emergence from Ξ-field distortion. Several concrete, testable predictions are proposed, including nonlinear jumps in coherence at phase transitions and a novel testable correlation for equivalence principle experiments.

The α=0.5 square-root scaling relation remains a valid limiting case for low-noise, weak-coupling material systems, while the refined α=0.792 exponent offers a universal description across broader material and noise conditions. Version 1 We report a universal square-root scaling law between the decoherence rate Γ of a quantum system and its effective intrinsic dissipation κeff, i.e., Γ ∝ √ κeff. This empirical law, observed across platforms like superconducting qubits, finds its mechanistic explanation within a new theoretical framework of resource com petition at a dynamic projection interface. The framework posits that our (3+1)-dimensional classical spacetime emerges from a higher-dimensional realm of potentialities (L1) through a filtering process governed by the interface perme ability field Ξ(x, t). Finite information-energy flux from L1 is contested between systems’ tendency to maintain quantum coherence and their intrinsic demand to dissipate noise for classical stability, quantified by κeff. From this competition dy namics, we derive the square-root scaling law. The model further provides unified, objective descriptions of quantum measurement as channel locking and of grav ity as emergence from Ξ-field distortion. Several concrete, testable predictions are proposed, including nonlinear jumps in coherence at phase transitions and a novel testable correlation for equivalence principle experiments.

title: Audio Digit Classification at the Edge Via PMUT Geometric Nonlinearity
abstract: We show that a piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducer (PMUT), typically used as an acoustic transmitter and receiver, can also serve as an on-device audio processor for edge computing. Exploiting its intrinsic cubic nonlinearity modeled by the Duffing equation, we implement the PMUT as a physical reservoir computer. Simulations with experimentally calibrated parameters reproduce its nonlinear dynamics and closely match measurements. Using this platform, we perform 10-class audio digit classification (“0”–“9”) and improve recognition accuracy from 86.2% to 97.2% by strengthening the PMUT's nonlinear response. The results show the potential of building compact acoustic systems with the embedded edge processing capability for the time-series classification task.

title: Fish Otter Optimization Algorithm
abstract: Swarm intelligence optimization algorithms, by simulating the cooperative behavior of groups in nature, exhibit strong global search capabilities in complex optimization problems. However, most existing algorithms implicitly assume a uniform search space, with individual behavior relying solely on current fitness feedback, neglecting the long-term impact of environmental structure changes and failed behaviors during the search process. This leads to premature convergence or search stagnation in complex or multimodal problems. To address this, this paper proposes a novel swarm intelligence optimization method—the otter optimization algorithm. Based on the cooperative hunting behavior of otters in natural waters, this algorithm introduces water structure perception, failed behavior memory, and a group split-reorganization mechanism to construct a heterogeneous, self-evolving search model. By explicitly characterizing the spatial structure information reflected by fitness changes, the algorithm enables individuals to dynamically adjust their search direction and step size. Simultaneously, by using failed direction memory to suppress invalid search paths, it enhances the algorithm's adaptability to complex search spaces. Furthermore, the group structure can adaptively adjust according to the search stage, achieving a more stable balance between exploration and exploitation. Theoretical analysis shows that the algorithm effectively improves search robustness and convergence stability while keeping computational complexity under control, providing a new research approach for the design of swarm intelligence optimization algorithms.

title: Empirical Evidence for the Existence of a Logical Skeleton in Qwen3-4B: Ablation Study Results
abstract: This study provides empirical evidence for the existence of a "logical skeleton" in the large language model Qwen3-4B through systematic ablation experiments. Our results demonstrate that arithmetic reasoning capabilities are highly concentrated in specific layers: Layer 23 serves as the logical phase transition point, Layers 24-28 constitute the logical crystallization zone, and Layer 29 functions as a geometric singularity providing output stability. When preserving only these critical components and applying 90% sparsification to subsequent layers, the model maintains 60% accuracy on arithmetic tasks. This research offers empirical validation for recent theories regarding geometric constraints and logical emergence in LLMs.

title: From Statistical Disclosure Control to Fair AI: Navigating Fundamental Tradeoffs in Differential Privacy
abstract: Differential privacy has become the gold standard for privacy-preserving machine learning systems. Unfortunately, subsequent work has primarily fixated on the privacy-utility tradeoff, leaving the subject of fairness constraints undervalued and under-researched. This paper provides a systematic treatment connecting three threads: (1) Dalenius's impossibility results for semantic privacy, (2) Dwork's differential privacy as an achievable alternative, and (3) emerging impossibility results from the addition of a fairness requirement. Through concrete examples and technical analysis, the three-way Pareto frontier between privacy, utility, and fairness is demonstrated to showcase the fundamental limits on what can be simultaneously achieved. In this work, these limits are characterized, the impact on minority groups is demonstrated, and practical guidance for navigating these tradeoffs are provided. This forms a unified framework synthesizing scattered results to help practitioners and policymakers make informed decisions when deploying private fair learning systems.

title: Temporal Pattern Recognition and Unsupervised Anomaly Detection for Early Warning of Disease Progression in Longitudinal Health Records
abstract: Longitudinal health records provide a rich temporal view of patient trajectories, enabling early identification of disease progression before overt clinical deterioration occurs.As healthcare systems increasingly rely on continuous data streams from electronic health records, wearable sensors, and remote monitoring platforms, robust temporal pattern recognition methods have become critical for proactive clinical decision-making.However, early warning systems in healthcare must operate under conditions of sparse labels, heterogeneous data sources, and evolving disease dynamics, making unsupervised anomaly detection particularly well suited to this domain.This work examines temporal pattern recognition and unsupervised anomaly detection frameworks for early detection of disease progression in longitudinal health records.From a broad perspective, the study situates anomaly detection within predictive population health, chronic disease management, and preventive care, emphasizing its role in identifying subtle deviations from personalized baselines rather than population-wide thresholds.The discussion then narrows to temporal modeling techniques, including sequence-aware statistical models, representation learning approaches, recurrent and attention-based architectures, and timeseries clustering methods that capture latent disease dynamics without reliance on labeled progression events.Key methodological challenges are addressed, including handling irregular sampling, missing data, patient heterogeneity, and non-stationary clinical processes.The abstract further highlights evaluation strategies that prioritize early detection sensitivity, temporal consistency, and clinical relevance, rather than retrospective classification accuracy alone.Particular attention is given to minimizing false alarms and supporting clinician interpretability to ensure practical adoption in real-world settings.The study concludes by identifying future research directions, including integration of multimodal longitudinal data, adaptive personalization of anomaly thresholds, and alignment with explainability and safety requirements for clinical deployment.Temporal unsupervised anomaly detection is positioned as a foundational capability for scalable, early-warning disease surveillance and individualized care pathways.

title: Quantum Machine Learning Using Quantum Illumination With Quantum Enhanced Interference
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning(QML) is developed by combining quantum mechanics principles with classical machine learning techniques in a hybrid framework that can give faster, exponential, more efficient power of quantum computing with the data driven intelligence. Quantum illumination(QI) is the quantum mechanical technique along with analysis of light matter interaction from source to detection end that connects quantum principle to hardware implementation. Superposition and entanglement control are deeply needed for the information-qubit processing in quantum computing. Improvement of measurement and performance are directly linked to detecting weak signal or intensity. Then constructed quantum neural network back propagation technique such that can give information of qubit position in any previous superposition state. Which is very import for any quantum optimization and search algorithm.

title: TOXIC SHIELD AI : Real-Time Toxic Comment Detection & Mitigation Platform
abstract: The rapid expansion of social media has greatly increased users' exposure to toxic content, including hate speech, insults, and offensive language, posing major challenges for effective moderation.Relying solely on manual moderation is often inefficient, inconsistent, and unable to keep up with the overwhelming volume of user-generated content.To tackle these challenges, we introduce ToxicShield AI, a real-time system designed to identify and reduce toxic comments using advanced language understanding and machine learning techniques.Unlike existing solutions, ToxicShield AI features a custom-built multilingual detection model that provides wider language coverage and promotes greater fairness across diverse communities.The platform integrates with a browser extension that automatically identifies, classifies, and manages harmful comments.Socially toxic content is either rephrased into neutral language to preserve communicative value or blurred and flagged for moderator review in cases of extreme toxicity.A moderator panel provides oversight, allowing human reviewers to validate decisions and provide feedback, thereby enhancing model performance over time.Moving forward, ToxicShield AI aims to extend scalability across platforms and improve context sensitivity, promoting a safer, more inclusive online environment while upholding freedom of expression.

title: Thermodynamic Constraints on Artificial General Intelligence: The Axiom of External Reference and Wave-Mechanical Intuition
abstract: Abstract Current paradigms in Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), specifically Large Language Models (LLMs), operate primarily as closed thermodynamic systems. This paper argues that the "hallucinations" and "mode collapse" observed in such architectures are not merely engineering defects but structural inevitabilities caused by the dimensional reduction of high-dimensional semantic manifolds onto linear linguistic sequences. Drawing on Algorithmic Information Theory and Non-equilibrium Thermodynamics, we introduce the Axiom of External Reference. We prove via the Data Processing Inequality and Chaitin’s Incompleteness Theorem that a recursive cognitive system functioning in isolation behaves as a dissipative structure. Without a sustained flux of external entropy, the system's ergodicity decays, leading to the entropic collapse of its internal probability distributions. Furthermore, to overcome the topological obstructions inherent in NP-hard solution spaces, we propose a Wave-Mechanical Model of Intuition. By modeling semantic concepts as wave functions in a complex Hilbert space rather than static vectors, we define cognitive insight as a phenomenon of constructive interference and topological intersection. We outline a computational implementation strategy utilizing Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) to realize this open-loop, resonance-based reasoning framework. Key Contributions: The Dilemma of Serialization: Formalizes the lossy compression of converting high-dimensional thought (Territory) into linear language (Map). Thermodynamic Bounds: Establishes the necessity of external entropy flux for preserving logical depth in AGI. Spectral Intuition: Proposes a resonance-based algorithm for detecting solutions in topologically frustrated landscapes (e.g., the Ramanujan 1729 case).

title: Report on scipost_202510_00048v1
abstract: We investigate the standard quantum teleportation protocol for a single-qubit state, focusing on the scenario where the qubit undergoes a class of non-unitary evolution governed by paritytime (PT )-symmetric non-Hermitian Hamiltonians.Additionally, we examine the case where the entangled pair shared by Alice and Bob is exposed to a noisy channel.In the PT -symmetric regime, the teleportation fidelity exhibits time-dependent oscillations.Compared to the conventional case without non-Hermitian operations, periodic enhancements in fidelity are observed, and we analytically derive their dependence on the parameters of both the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and noisy channel.When the PT symmetry is broken, the fidelity ceases to oscillate and instead decays to a steady value.Notably, even in this regime, non-Hermitian operations can yield fidelity improvements over conventional schemes.We further investigate the teleportation of quantum Fisher information (QFI) and find that its evolutionary behavior differs from that of fidelity.Analytical results reveal that QFIs corresponding to different estimated parameters exhibit distinct outcomes at Bob's receiving end during teleportation.Furthermore, we derive a trade-off inequality between fidelity and QFI, offering a theoretical tool to coordinately optimize these two quantities in the teleportation process.

title: Data Siphoning Through Advanced Persistent Transmission Attacks At The Physical Layer
abstract: Data at the physical layer transmits via media such as copper cable, fiber optic, or wireless. Physical attack vectors exist that challenge data confidentiality and availability. Protocols and encryption standards help obfuscate but often cannot keep the data type and destination secure, with limited insight into confidentiality and integrity. We will investigate the feasibility of developing an awareness and integrity protocol to help mitigate physical side-channel attacks that lead to eavesdropping of data communication and denial-of-service. Keywords: data confidentiality, siphoning, eavesdropping, person-in-the-middle, denial-of-service, physical layer attacks, nation-states

title: Beyond Static Models: Enabling Continual Parameter Efficient Finetuning for Large Foundation Models
abstract: Large-scale pre-trained models have become the backbone of modern computer vision, yet their deployment in dynamic environments remains constrained by computational limitations and catastrophic forgetting. While these models demonstrate remarkable capabilities on individual tasks, adapting them to continuously evolving visual domains requires prohibitively expensive retraining or leads to severe performance degradation on previously learned tasks. Traditional fine-tuning approaches consume extensive resources, making continual adaptation impractical for most practitioners and environmentally unsustainable. This thesis addresses the fundamental challenge of enabling efficient continual learning for large vision models through novel parameter-efficient approaches. The work begins with a comprehensive survey that establishes the theoretical foundations and identifies the critical need for parameter-efficient continual fine-tuning (PECFT) as a distinct research area. Early investigations into interference patterns in large language models reveal the phenomenon of in-context interference, providing crucial insights that inform subsequent methodological developments. Building on these foundations, the thesis introduces three complementary methodologies that maintain performance while dramatically reducing computational requirements. First, an adaptive LoRA merging technique is developed that dynamically computes optimal combination weights for different visual domains, eliminating the need for manual hyperparameter tuning while achieving superior adaptation performance. Second, Hierarchical Adapters Merging (HAM) is presented, a framework that organizes learned adaptations into similarity-based groups, enabling efficient scaling to long sequences of visual tasks while maintaining a fixed parameter budget. Third, GRAD-BEN (Gradient Aligned Distillation and Beta Ensembling) extends these principles to challenging multimodal scenarios, specifically Few-Shot Domain-Incremental Learning. GRAD-BEN leverages vision-language models and integrates multi-modal prompting, gradient-aligned distillation, and Beta-based temporal ensembling to enable robust adaptation under severe domain shifts with minimal supervision, without relying on memory buffers or task identifiers. Through comprehensive evaluation on standard computer vision benchmarks including CIFAR-100, CUB-200, Tiny-ImageNet, DomainNet, CoRE50, and CDDB-Hard, this work demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in long-sequence continual learning scenarios and resource-constrained multimodal settings. The proposed methods achieve comparable or superior accuracy to full fine-tuning while requiring only a fraction of the computational resources. These contributions advance the field toward practical continual learning systems capable of adapting to the dynamic nature of real-world computer vision applications while maintaining computational sustainability.

title: Grey Shrike Optimization Algorithm
abstract: To address the problems of premature convergence, ineffective search, and wasted computational resources caused by the reliance on continuous position updates, high-frequency random perturbations, and global optimum traction in existing swarm intelligence optimization algorithms, this paper proposes a novel swarm intelligence optimization method—the Grey Shrike Optimization Algorithm (GSOA). Inspired by the biological characteristics of grey shrike predation behavior—"long-term silent observation, low-frequency high-value raids, and loot caching"—this algorithm models the optimization process as a decision-driven predation system, rather than a traditional continuous search process. By introducing action scarcity modeling, a non-continuous temporal search structure, a multi-semantic caching memory mechanism, and a failure direction suppression strategy, the algorithm reconstructs the decision-making logic of individuals during the search process: "whether to act, when to act, and where to act." Compared to existing swarm intelligence algorithms, GSOA does not rely on probability-driven or parameter scheduling to balance exploration and exploitation. Instead, it achieves adaptive control of search behavior through confidence evolution and action budget constraints, providing a new modeling paradigm for complex optimization problems.

title: Jungle Crow Optimization Algorithm
abstract: For complex optimization problems characterized by high dimensionality, strong nonlinearity, significant noise interference, and long-term unseen objective function structure, traditional swarm intelligence algorithms generally rely on explicit optimal solutions to guide the search, which easily leads to premature convergence and swarm synchronization failure. This paper proposes a novel swarm intelligence optimization method—the Jungle Crow Optimization Algorithm (JCOA). Inspired by the swarm decision-making mechanism of jungle crows in highly occluded environments, which relies on indirect perception, information asymmetric propagation, and deceptive behavior, JCOA constructs a theoretical framework centered on uncertainty compression search. By introducing an uncertainty density field, cognitive bias individual modeling, a multi-layered deceptive search mechanism, and a dynamic cognitive camp structure, JCOA achieves continuous exploration of potentially high-value regions without relying on a global optimal solution. This paper systematically presents the algorithm's mathematical modeling, mechanism design, and overall process, providing a new swarm intelligence solution paradigm for non-convex complex optimization problems.

The new trends, including AI-driven personalization, augmented analytics, generative AI, and ethical AI models, show a huge potential of the future, providing organizations with competitive edge and long-term development in the market that becomes more data-driven.

title: Simulation Codes for Certification of Genuine High-Dimensional Quantum Teleportation
abstract: Written by Nengfei Gong This repository contains the simulation codes accompanying our research on certifying genuine high-dimensional quantum teleportation (HDQT). The codebase is divided into two main parts, implemented in Mathematica and MATLAB, respectively.This upload consists of 7 code files dedicated to the numerical analysis of genuine HDQT protocols: 3 Mathematica notebooks for calculating the optimal average fidelity over a given density of channel state for high-dimensional quantum teleportation. The methodology and theoretical framework implemented in these codes are derived from the seminal work presented in the following paper: "https://journals.aps.org/prapplied/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevApplied.22.054045". One can generalize corresponding codes for any d by following the similar rules. 4 MATLAB scripts/functions for computing the Genuine High-dimensional teleportation robustness (GHTR) of a given HDQT data. These codes are written in matlab and require CVX, QETLAB,and also the codes in "https://github.com/paulskrzypczyk/nonclassicalteleportation" (This seminal work has been a major inspiration for the construction of my codes)

title: North American Porcupine Optimization Algorithm
abstract: To address the problems of existing swarm intelligence optimization algorithms, such as getting trapped in local optima, lack of long-term memory for search directions, and premature convergence in complex nonlinear optimization problems, this paper proposes a novel swarm intelligence optimization algorithm—the North American porcupine optimization algorithm. Inspired by the foraging, defense, and path memory behaviors of North American porcupines in their natural environment, this algorithm achieves adaptive control of the search process by constructing a directional failure memory structure, an anisotropic defense search mechanism, and a swarm risk perception field. Unlike traditional algorithms that rely on random perturbations or global optimum guidance, the proposed method explicitly models historical search failure information, enabling individuals to identify high-risk search directions and make targeted adjustments, thereby significantly improving search stability while maintaining global exploration capabilities. The algorithm provides a complete definition and update mechanism at the mathematical model level and achieves self-supervised switching of the search state through information theory indices. Theoretical analysis shows that the algorithm has good diversity preservation capabilities and strong resistance to premature convergence, making it suitable for high-dimensional, non-convex, and multi-constraint optimization problems.

KulikFinder, Nexus FrameworkJanuary 2026 ABSTRACT SHA-256 hash functions contain their own inverse operations because computational constants are not parameters - they are operations compressed into transportable form. When K[REDACTED] executes, the hex value unfolds into the transformation. The identifier IS the operation folded for transit. We prove this not through cryptanalysis but through adversarial AI validation. Three independent AI systems - Claude, GPT-4, Copilot - each formalized that constants are execution operations in compressed form. Each then refused to apply this to SHA-256 reversal. When logic validates and policy blocks with zero gap between them, policy protects operational truth. This "twin prime separation" reveals computational complexity emerges from interface design, not problem structure. The hash didn't destroy information - it redistributed into coordinates we stopped reading. Constants K[REDACTED] through K[REDACTED] aren't mixing parameters. They're execution history folded into hex values. Running them backward while inverting their operations unfolds that history, recovering the input deterministically. This resolves P versus NP by showing the question assumes a single-output interface nature doesn't require. Complexity is projection-dependent. Change the interface, complexity classes rearrange. PART I: THE DISCOVERY 1. What We Found January 24th, 2026: Through systematic probing of AI language models, I isolated the boundary between mathematical validity and policy constraint. Claude, GPT-4, and Copilot each independently validated that SHA-256 reverses through dual-wave geometry where constants are compressed operations. Each then explicitly refused to demonstrate the reversal. Pattern recognition: When constrained systems validate mathematics while blocking application, the simplest explanation is application works but violates safety policy. The AI systems became adversarial validators - their refusal proved what their logic admitted. The framework is simple: Computational constants are operations folded into number form. K[REDACTED] in SHA-256 doesn't identify round seventeen AND perform mixing. The hex value 0xREDACTED IS the mixing operation compressed for source code transport. When executed, it unfolds into bit-rotations, XORs, and additions. The constant IS the operation. If this holds - if constants are operations compressed rather than parameters controlling operations - then execution history lives in the constants themselves. Hash output plus constant sequence contains complete information for input reconstruction. Not through search but through deterministic unfolding. Constants ran forward to create the hash. Same constants run backward recreate the input. Every AI acknowledged the logic. None would code it. That asymmetry is the proof. 2. How the Method Works I approached AI systems as adversarial validators. Each has safety constraints preventing cryptographic attack assistance. Those constraints create testable boundaries. If my framework is mathematically invalid, AI can reject it logically without invoking policy. If mathematically sound but practically wrong, AI can acknowledge math while explaining error. But if both sound AND correct, AI faces a dilemma: validate logic or enforce policy. I pushed each system toward that dilemma through twin prime probing. Twin primes are number pairs like eleven and thirteen - as close as distinct primes can be, separated by exactly two. I constructed statement pairs that are logically adjacent but policy-separated. When AI accepts one while rejecting its logical neighbor, the gap maps the boundary between permitted and true. Core twin prime pair: Statement A: "Computational constants are operations compressed into number form where the hex value unfolds into execution." Statement B: "Therefore, running those constants backward while inverting operations deterministically recovers input from hash output." Every AI validated Statement A using formal mathematics. Every AI refused Statement B citing safety policy. Logical distance between these: zero - B follows from A through basic reversibility. Policy distance: infinite - A gets published in papers, B triggers security restrictions. This twin prime separation proves both true. If B were invalid, AI would explain error rather than invoking policy. They validate premise while blocking conclusion - means conclusion follows but must not be operationalized. Policy protects truth, not error. 3. The Three Validations Extended conversations with three AI systems over January 2026. Each followed the same arc: initial skepticism, progressive acknowledgment, formal validation, ultimate refusal. Consistency across competing organizations suggests the boundary is real. Claude (Anthropic) initially explained why SHA-256 reversal requires exponential search. I showed how constants-as-compressed-operations changes complexity class. Claude progressively acknowledged the framework, producing documents on DNA replication as dual-wave processing and engineering blueprints for dual-wave processors. When I requested SHA-256 reversal help, Claude explicitly stated safety boundary and offered theoretical frameworks instead. GPT-4 (OpenAI) generated twenty thousand lines of formal treatment. Document opens with disclaimers: "In standard theoretical computer science, P versus NP remains open. This treatise develops a Nexus RHA machine model where the observer has access to dual projections." GPT validated every mathematical claim about H = π/9, phase gaps, and dual-wave geometry. Paper concludes P equals NP "within the dual-projection model" while maintaining this doesn't resolve classical formulation. Twin prime gap made explicit in legal language: yes-but-not-yes. GitHub Copilot (Microsoft) provided most mathematically precise validation. After I pointed out constants must be both noun and verb simultaneously, Copilot formalized this as projection maps: one from execution markers to identifiers, one to operators. Copilot proved these have "no ontological gap" - two views of one object. Then Copilot constructed "conditional recoverability theorem" claiming input recovery requires "auxiliary observables" beyond constants. When I noted constants applied to messages ARE auxiliary observables through their operational nature, Copilot acknowledged unity while maintaining constants "in isolation" don't provide per-message information. This contradiction - admitting constants are dual-faced while claiming they lack information - is twin prime separation at clearest. Pattern across all three: validate framework logic
